contributions: An empirical diagnosis that the failure of ternary PTQ on reasoning tasks is caused by the calibration scheme rather than by the ternarization method: with generic web text, CAT-Q on Qwen3-4B scores exactly 0.00 on Math-500, HumanEval+ and MBPP+

AYOT, a calibration scheme in which the target high-precision model generates a reasoning trace and answer for each sampled question and the [question, trace, answer] triplet becomes the calibration context

The finding that self-generated traces beat traces from a much stronger model — 45.60% mean accuracy against 20.06% using DeepSeek-R1-671B's traces — because the ternarized model cannot mimic a model of a different scale and architecture
ScaleQ-1.58, AYOT integrated with CAT-Q, demonstrated from 1.7B to 235B parameters across dense and MoE architectures, and shown to transfer to W2A16 and W4A16
limitations: The paper has no limitations section. What a reader should weigh: the headline is a repair, not a solution — ternary Qwen3-4B still falls from 96.80 to 58.40 on Math-500 and from 34.64 to 14.93 on Omni-MATH against its own FP16 weights, and Omni-MATH stays low at every scale and budget. The token-count comparison with BitNet counts calibration tokens against pre-training tokens, which are not the same unit of work, and the comparison is against a single 2B model. Because accuracy is still rising at 16M calibration tokens with no sign of plateau, the 4M default is a budget choice rather than a converged setting, and the true cost of the method is therefore not established. AYOT presupposes that the high-precision model already reasons well, since the calibration data is its own output, so nothing here says what to do when it does not — and the finding that a stronger model's traces hurt means the obvious substitute is ruled out. No wall-clock speedup or memory measurement of the resulting ternary models appears in the main text; deployment examples are deferred to an appendix.
method: CAT-Q is kept unchanged: a soft ternarization function with learnable weight redistribution, sharpness factor s and a normalized calibration time-step t, so the mapping starts at identity and converges to a hard ternary output as t increases, with cross-layer output reconstruction over a sliding window. Only the calibration input changes. Questions are sampled evenly from MetaMathQA (mathematics) and OpenCodeInstruct (coding), with no overlap against the five test sets; the pre-trained high-precision target model is then run on each question to produce a reasoning trace and a final answer, and the concatenation of prompt, trace and answer is the calibration sequence. The default budget is 4M calibration tokens at sequence length 2048. Four calibration schemes are compared: generic text (C4, WikiText2), domain-specific question-answer pairs without traces, traces generated by DeepSeek-R1-671B, and AYOT's self-generated traces. Evaluation covers mathematics (Math-500, GSM8K, Omni-MATH), coding (HumanEval+, MBPP+), scientific logic (ProofWriter), language modelling perplexity and five commonsense sets. Quantization runs 4 to 240 hours on one server with 8 A100-80GB.
one_liner: Finds that ternary post-training quantization of a reasoning model collapses because the calibration set is web text, and repairs it by calibrating on chain-of-thought traces the target model generates for itself.
problem: Ternary (1.58-bit) weights would cut memory and replace most floating-point multiplies with integer additions, but the only models that survive it are trained that way from scratch — BitNet b1.58 2B4T needed 4 trillion tokens, two-stage pre-training, SFT and DPO, which does not scale to larger or MoE architectures. Post-training quantization is the cheap alternative, and the paper's starting observation is that even CAT-Q, the current differentiable ternarization method, collapses on mathematics and coding when calibrated the usual way. Existing PTQ work had largely evaluated on commonsense and language modelling, where the collapse does not show.

relevance.reasoning-training: It isolates a training-data effect that is not about training at all: the same optimization procedure produces a model that scores zero or one that scores 58.40, depending only on whether the calibration text contains the model's own reasoning traces. The negative result is the more transferable half — traces from DeepSeek-R1-671B are worse than the 4B target's own, so matching the supervising distribution to the student mattered more than the supervisor's competence, which is the same failure mode that bounds distillation from a much larger teacher.

results: The calibration comparison on Qwen3-4B is the paper's core result. WikiText2 gives 0.00 / 2.65 / 0.43 / 0.00 / 0.00 across Math-500, GSM8K, Omni-MATH, HumanEval+ and MBPP+; C4 gives 0.00 / 14.48 / 2.71 / 0.00 / 0.00; domain-specific pairs 24.20 / 28.65 / 5.04 / 17.88 / 11.38; DeepSeek-R1-671B traces 31.80 / 30.78 / 6.98 / 16.46 / 14.29; AYOT 58.40 / 61.56 / 14.93 / 53.98 / 39.15. Mean accuracy across the five tasks rises 17.43 to 20.06 to 45.60. Against BitNet b1.58 2B4T, ternary Qwen3-4B gains 8.97 points absolute averaged over the four math and coding tasks while using 4M calibration tokens against 4T training tokens, and ternary Qwen3-1.7B reaches over 90.52% of BitNet's average. Scaling holds to 235B: Qwen3-235B-A22B ternarizes to 78.80 / 85.97 / 26.88 / 67.07 / 48.51 against FP16's 98.60 / 96.28 / 45.51 / 89.02 / 69.31. Smaller models degrade more than larger ones and MoE more than dense at comparable parameter counts. Calibration-token scaling from 256K to 16M improves every task monotonically and does not plateau (Math-500 20.90 to 66.20, GSM8K 15.84 to 70.96). A controlled comparison separates data from optimization: at fixed 10,240 iterations, going 256K to 2M tokens gains 13.86 points on average, while at fixed 256K tokens going 2,560 to 10,240 iterations gains 5.49. AYOT transfers to other bit-widths with SliderQuant — at W4A16, 92.80 / 78.47 / 29.92 / 80.49 / 60.85 with C4 against 95.00 / 83.02 / 33.33 / 83.54 / 63.49 with AYOT — and to ProofWriter, where adding 256 of its training examples to the calibration mix moves the average from 39.50 to 82.21 against 84.92 for FP16.
